title: How Emotion Changes What You See
author: Cristian Damian
summary: Damian examines why the same set of facts can produce wildly different interpretations depending on a person's emotional state, arguing that feeling is not a reaction to what we observe but a filter that shapes what we notice in the first place. Using the example of an unanswered message that curdles from a minor annoyance into an imagined slight over the course of a day, he shows how fear narrows attention onto perceived threats while anger actively invents motives and intentions that the available evidence cannot support. He connects this to his recurring idea of the 'Reality Gap' -- the distance between what is actually happening and the internal map a person builds of it -- arguing that emotional states distort that map even when no new information has arrived. Crucially, Damian notes that a distorted map does not feel distorted; it feels like unusual clarity and certainty, which is exactly why the error goes undetected in the moment. His practical advice is to separate action from interpretation: act on deadlines as needed, but delay concluding anything about a person's character or intent until the emotional state has passed.
points: Damian's central claim: 'You don't feel angry about what you saw. You see it through the anger' -- emotion shapes perception before conscious reasoning ever gets a turn.
Fear produces tunnel vision 'built for a predator, pointed at a calendar invite' -- narrowing attention onto a perceived threat even when the threat is trivial, like a routine email.

Anger doesn't just intensify a reaction, it invents unsupported motives: assigning a colleague's oversight to deliberate malice adds detail and confidence that nothing in the evidence actually supports.
The tell that a map is distorted is that it feels like clarity, not confusion -- certainty that arrives fast and feels great is the thing to check.
Practical takeaway: separate the action from the interpretation -- answer the email or make the call, but don't decide what kind of person someone is until the emotional state has passed.
quotes: You don't feel angry about what you saw. You see it through the anger. Most of us picture this the other way around.
Fear collapses your attention onto the threat, and whatever isn't the threat stops making it onto the map. You're not choosing this.
Anger doesn't only make it feel worse. It supplies a reason for it. Where fear left things off your map, this puts something on it that was never there.
That certainty is the giveaway, because you have no access to the inside of anyone's head. If your map has their reasoning on it, your map has fiction on it.
The experience of having a distorted map is not the experience of distortion. It's the experience of clarity. Sharper than usual, more certain than usual, everything suddenly fitting together.
The move is smaller. When you notice the state, go ahead and act. Send the reply, make the call, handle the thing. Just don't conclude yet.
Answer the email. Don't decide what kind of person they are.
